endings.text: You went through the square and up to the Water Tower. You saw the city's big bell and its pumps in one afternoon. The note got there. Tomorrow night the Opera House opens. You walk home as the lamps come on, with the wind at your back.

You went through the square and down to the river. You saw the bell tower, and then the black ruins of last night's fire. The note got there. The tired firemen are going home to sleep, and so are you. The wind is still blowing hard.
You went the long way by LaSalle Street, and then up to the Water Tower. The note got there, and almost every seat for tomorrow night is sold. You get home just as the sun goes down.

You went the long way by LaSalle Street, and then down to the river, where people are still looking at the ruins. The note got there. Tomorrow the Opera House opens at last. You go home as the sun sets.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. II, 'Hotel History', pp. 502-503, the paragraph beginning 'The Sherman House was built in 1836-37'; museum, landmark 'Sherman House', captions 'View from Court House Cupola, North' and 'Sherman House before the Fire'.
evidence.text: Andreas (1885): 'The Sherman House was built in 1836-37, by Hon. F. C. Sherman, who was subsequently Mayor of Chicago', first called the City Hotel; in 1844 Sherman added two stories and renamed it. In May 1861 it was torn down for a new hotel, opened on 8 July 1861: 'The new Sherman House was six stories high, and had a frontage of one hundred and eighty feet on Clark, and one hundred and fifty feet on Randolph Street, the latter overlooking the public square. The material of the structure was the finest Athens marble, from the quarries at Lemont'. The museum: Francis C. Sherman 'served two terms as Chicago's mayor in the early 1860s'; 'The hotel's main entrance was on Clark Street, through a two-story portico.'

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. II, 'Music and Drama', p. 607, the announcement beginning 'The season at the Opera House'; museum, landmark 'Sherman House', the caption quoting William Gallagher's letter.
evidence.text: The Opera House's announcement, printed by Andreas: 'The season at the Opera House will be inaugurated on Monday, October 9 [1871], by Theodore Thomas, with his concert organization of sixty performers, who will give a series of ten grand symphony and popular concerts.' After the fire William Gallagher wrote to his sister: 'Theodore Thomas was at the Sherman House with his orchestra,' and 'was to have commenced his concerts on the Monday night after the fire. He was compelled to run for his life'.

evidence.locator: Landmark 'Court House', captions 'Courthouse Square' (ichi-62080) and 'The Court House Shortly Before the Fire' (ichi-64281); landmark 'Sherman House', caption 'Sherman House before the Fire' (the fence).
evidence.text: The museum: the 1853 Court House and City Hall 'occupied ... the entire downtown block formed by Randolph, Clark, Washington, and LaSalle streets', its footprint small enough 'to allow the block to include a good deal of landscaping, which gave what was called Court House Square the appearance of a park.' It was 'originally two stories and an above-ground basement'; the city 'soon added a third floor and the cupola, with a spiral staircase leading to an observatory balcony 120 feet high, which served as a fire watchman's walk.' 'By the time of the fire the Court House had also added east and west wings, a brand-new clock, and a 10,849-pound bronze bell'. It 'housed virtually all city and country offices, from the jail in its basement to the mayor's quarters, the debtors' prison, the city council, the board of public works, and the courtrooms on the upper floors.' 'The designer of the 1853 structure was John M. Van Osdel, who also built the previous court house.' A fence 'enclosed Court House Square'.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. II, 'The Burning of Chicago', pp. 709-711: the report's paragraph beginning 'The first information received by the Fire Department', and the statements of William J. Brown and Mathias Schaffer.
evidence.text: The Board of Police and Fire Commissioners' report, printed by Andreas: the first alarm 'was given by Mathias Schaffer, from the Court-house cupola, he being the night watchman on duty at the time, and having sighted the fire.' Schaffer's own statement, as Andreas condenses it: 'Observing it through his spy-glass, he located the scene near the corner of Canalport Avenue and Halsted Street, and rang up the night operator, signaling him to give Box 342. Brown struck the alarm. A short time after that, Schaefer called to Brown, and told him the fire was not so far off; but as the engines would have to pass the spot, it was decided not to send a different alarm'. Andreas: 'The error made by Mr. Schaffer consisted in not sounding a correct alarm, when his mistake was discovered by himself. Had he done so, several engines not in service under the call of 342 would have been brought out.' William J. Brown was the night operator. The fire-alarm telegraph office was 'in the Court-house tower'.

evidence.locator: Landmark 'Chamber of Commerce', caption 'Chamber of Commerce' (ichi-63073); landmark 'Court House', second caption.
evidence.text: The museum: 'The Chamber of Commerce dedicated its new building on August 30, 1865. The building was designed by Edward Burling. Charles Randolph, President of the Board of Trade, delivered the main address of the day. By far the most important business conducted in this building, whose grand hall was decorated with frescoes and paintings, was the commodities exchange overseen by the Board.' It stood on the southeast corner of LaSalle and Washington streets, just south of Court House Square.

evidence.locator: p. 138, the paragraph continuing from 'Up to about 1868'.
evidence.text: Colbert and Chamberlin (1871): after 1868 'Lasalle Street was improved, and became popular as the home of Insurance Companies and commission merchants, while the banks moved toward that and Washington Street, as the newspapers were gathering on and near Dearborn.'

evidence.locator: Museum, landmark 'Crosby's Opera House', the captions 'Crosby's Opera House' (ichi-62079); Andreas vol. II, 'Music and Drama', pp. 603-607.
evidence.text: The museum: Crosby's Opera House 'stood for less than six-and-a-half years on the north side of Washington Street between State and Dearborn.' Its builder Uranus Crosby and the architect W. W. Boyington 'erected this five-story Italianate palace, topped with a mansard roof. Allegorical statues of Painting, Sculpture, Music, and Commerce (after all, this was Chicago)' stood over its entry arch. The first floor held shops, 'including music publishers Root & Cady ..., the piano store of W. W. Kimball, and the confectioner and restauranteur H. M. Kinsley'; in the rear was the opera house itself, 'with seats for three thousand patrons.' It opened in April 1865. 'By early 1871 he made plans for a major renovation of the theater, which took place that summer. The much anticipated re-opening was scheduled for October 9, with a concert led by maestro Theodore Thomas.' Andreas names him Uranus H. Crosby, and says the proprietary interest had since passed to Albert Crosby.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. II, 'Music and Drama', p. 607, the paragraphs beginning 'During the summer of 1871' and 'The Tribune of October 8, 1871, remarked'.
evidence.text: Andreas (1885): 'During the summer of 1871, Crosby's Opera House underwent material alterations', 'the cost of the improvements being stated at about $80,000.' 'The Tribune of October 8, 1871, remarked: "The decorators and upholsterers are still busy putting the finishing touches on the Opera House. * * * The house is virtually ready, with the exception of the locating of the large bronzes and a few other ornaments and the laying down of the carpets." ... "The box-office sheets are crossed to an extent which indicates that the whole house, gallery and all, is nearly sold for the first night."'

evidence.locator: pp. 94-95, the paragraph beginning 'The Crosby Opera House, had been closed'.
evidence.text: Sheahan and Upton (1871): 'The Crosby Opera House, had been closed during the summer and fall for renovation. Its proprietor had expended $80,000 upon it in ornamentation, upholstery and frescoing. It was to have been re-opened to the public on Monday evening, the night after the fire, by the Theodore Thomas orchestral troupe, and on Sunday evening, only an hour or two before the fire, it was lit up for the first time, that its effects might be seen by gaslight.'

evidence.locator: Landmark 'Water Tower', captions 'Laying of the cornerstone for the Water Tower, March 25, 1867' (ichi-64424) and 'Chicago Water Works' (ichi-06859).
evidence.text: The museum: 'Designed by W. W. Boyington and dedicated at a great celebration in March of 1867', the waterworks had 'the limestone Water Tower and Pumping Station on either side of Pine Street (now Michigan Avenue) at Chicago Avenue, and a two-mile tunnel beneath the lake, at the end of which was an intake known as the "crib."' The Board of Public Works called the style 'castellated Gothic'. City Engineer Ellis S. Chesbrough proposed the works 'to draw water from far enough out in the lake so that it would not be contaminated by the unspeakably polluted Chicago River'. The cornerstone of the Water Tower was laid on 25 March 1867.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. II, 'The Burning of Chicago', p. 710, the report's paragraphs beginning 'The single set of pumping works' and 'The Board of Police have, year by year'.
evidence.text: The Board of Police and Fire Commissioners' report (printed by Andreas): 'The single set of pumping works, upon which the salvation of the city depended, were roofed with wood, had no appliance by which water could be raised to the roof in case of fire, and was one of the earliest buildings to burn in the North Division.' The Board had warned 'year by year' that 'the water supply was insufficient', that 'our fire hydrants were twice too far apart', that 'wooden cornices were an abomination', and that the city should not be left 'to the mercy of chance, or accident, with a single set.' 'None of these things was noticed by the mayor, the Common Council, or the newspapers.'

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. II, 'The Burning of Chicago', pp. 705-706, the paragraphs beginning 'Some time between ten and eleven' and 'In the rear of the planing mill'; museum, landmark 'Saturday Night Fire' and timeline entry 'A Fiery Prelude' (1871-10-07).
evidence.text: Andreas (1885): 'Some time between ten and eleven o'clock, on Saturday night', an alarm from Box 248 called the Fire Department to No. 209 South Canal Street, where 'a fire was raging in the boiler-room of Lull & Holmes's planing mill'. 'The greater portion of the block was filled with lumber, sheds, outbuildings, and dwelling houses'. The museum: it burned 'well into Sunday afternoon', by which time 'four square blocks and close to a million dollars in property had gone up in smoke'; the neighbourhood 'was popularly known to insurance brokers as the "Red Flash" because of the combustibility of the local buildings and their contents', and the fire 'left Chicago's already undermanned and underequipped firefighters critically shorthanded and overtired, and some of their equipment badly damaged.' The Great Fire would erupt 'about twenty-four hours later and ten blocks to the south.'

evidence.locator: pp. 63-64, the paragraphs ending the account of the Saturday fire.
evidence.text: Sheahan and Upton (1871): 'Between Canal street and the river were a number of coal yards, and the extensive lumber yard of Chapin & Foss. The piles of coal and lumber burned all day on Sunday, and when night set in the sky reflected the brilliant light of the blazing mass below.' 'The neighborhood was visited during the day by thousands of persons. About one hundred families were turned out of their homes by the fire.'

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. II, p. 710, the report's paragraph beginning 'The firemen and their officers were sober'.
evidence.text: The Board's report (printed by Andreas): 'A large part of the Department had worked on Saturday night, and Sunday until 3 p.m. — eighteen hours' steady work, — and they were nearly exhausted when this fire commenced'.

evidence.locator: 'Weather Prior to the Fire' (The Months Leading Up to the Fire; The Week Leading Up to the Fire) and 'Weather During the Fire: October 8th'; the Overview's paragraph on the lost station records.
evidence.text: The National Weather Service's reconstruction: from 7 July to 8 October 1871 'only 3.55 inches of precipitation were recorded'; 'From September 29th through October 8th, Chicago saw no precipitation at all.' On 8 October highs were 'in the low to mid 80s across most of northern Illinois', and 'southwest winds peaked at around 35 to 45 mph, including within the city of Chicago.' Chicago's own weather records were lost in the fire.

The messenger the visitor plays, their age and work for the hotel, the note for the Opera House and its delivery, the route, the two choices, the four endings, the hour at each stop, the timing inputs and the A Sunday Errand keepsake are invented connective narrative. No such messenger or note is recorded; no named person is met or speaks, and the walk ends at dusk, before the fire of that night.

keepsake.text: A made-up messenger's slip for one Sunday afternoon in October 1871: which way you went to the Opera House, and where you watched the sun go down. No real messenger or note is written on it.
keepsake.title: A Sunday Errand

opening.text:
JAUNT: A MESSAGE FOR THE OPERA HOUSE. It is Sunday, 8 October 1871. You are thirteen, and you carry messages for the Sherman House, a big hotel on Clark Street. A hotel is open every day, even on Sunday. Today the clerk gives you a folded note. It must get to Crosby's Opera House before dark.

You pick the way. The streets and the buildings are real. The messenger is you.

cemetery_dead_house_1871.text: A little house in the cemetery where bodies were kept before burial. On Monday evening, with the crowd all around it, it caught fire. People shuddered, but it was empty, and it burned to the ground.

chamber_of_commerce_1871.text: The Board of Trade's home, built of pale stone facing the Court House square. Grain was traded in a great hall upstairs, 44 feet high. Banks and merchants rented the floors below.

chicago_pumping_station_1871.text: The engine house pulled water through a tunnel two miles under the lake and up the tower. Its roof caught fire at 3:20 in the morning. Then the city had no water to fight the fire.

chicago_water_tower_1871.text: A castle of yellow Joliet stone hiding an iron pipe 138 feet tall. The pumps across the street forced lake water up it so the city's mains kept an even pressure.

cook_county_court_house_1871.text: The city and the county shared this marble building from 1853. In 1870 two big stone wings and another storey were added. Its cupola held the fire watch and the city's great bell.

court_house_square_1871.text: The open square round the Court House. The building stood in the middle, back from the streets, behind an iron fence on a stone base. Trees and lamps stood along the walks.

crosbys_opera_house_1871.text: Uranus Crosby's grand opera house, with an art gallery, a concert hall and shops. It cost about $600,000 and opened in April 1865. It burned in the fire, days before it was to reopen.

dalton_cottage_1871.text: A one-storey frame cottage next door to the O'Learys, raised on cedar posts four feet off the ground. It stood only a few steps from the barn and burned in the first minutes.

dalton_shed_1871.text: A board shed at the back of Dalton's lot, right beside the O'Leary barn. A high fence joined it to Dalton's house.

field_leiter_1871.text: Marshall Field and Levi Leiter's dry goods store, in Potter Palmer's marble building on State Street. Its clerks sprayed it with its own pumps through the night. When the city's water failed, it burned.

forbes_cottage_1871.text: A frame house in two parts, two doors from the O'Learys. The Forbes family lived in front; the Lee and Connovan families rented the back.

lake_shore_sands_1871.text: Open sand between the town and the lake. When the North Side burned, all kinds of people crowded down here. Judges and merchants sat beside workingmen and their families, with the water at their backs.

ogden_house_1871.text: Mahlon D. Ogden's big wooden house stood in its grounds on Washington Square. Everything around it burned. With the family away, friends covered it with wet blankets and carpets, and in the morning it still stood.

old_city_cemetery_1871.text: Most of the bodies had been moved away, but old headstones and grassy mounds still stood in the long grass. On Monday about thirty thousand people crowded in here with trunks, chairs and bundles, watching the North Side burn.

oleary_barn_1871.text: A small wooden barn where the O'Learys kept five cows. The Great Chicago Fire began here on Sunday night. Legend says a cow kicked over a lamp, but the inquiry could not prove how it started.

oleary_cottage_1871.text: Two little frame houses, one behind the other. The McLaughlins rented the front one and had a party that night. The O'Learys and their five children lived in the back, and the wind spared both houses.

palmer_house_1871.text: Potter Palmer's first hotel, eight storeys with stone fronts on State Street. It opened in September 1870, barely a year before the fire. At four in the morning it was the last great hotel standing.

pumping_works_grounds_1871.text: The open ground in front of the pumping works. The engine house stood back from the street behind an iron railing. No houses stood between it and Chicago Avenue.

sherman_house_1871.text: One of the city's two great hotels, six storeys of pale Lemont stone looking over the Court House square. Over three hundred guests slept here the night of the fire.

st_michaels_church_1871.text: The German Catholic parish had just finished this huge brick church, with a tower and a chime of bells. The fire burned its roof and steeple, and the bells crashed down. But the walls were built so well that they stood.

sullivan_house_1871.text: The house across the street from the O'Learys. Dennis Sullivan sat by its fence when he saw the barn burning. He ran across to help.

tremont_house_1871.text: The third Tremont House, five and a half storeys of brick on Lake and Dearborn. It opened in 1850 and was one of the city's great hotels. It burned in the small hours of 9 October 1871.

tribune_building_1871.text: The Chicago Tribune's own building, four storeys of Joliet marble with iron frames and roof. People thought it could not burn. At four in the morning it was the only newspaper office still standing, but it burned after daylight.

washington_square_1871.text: An open square of grass in front of the Ogden house. People fleeing the fire crowded in with their belongings. The heat drove them on, and the things they left behind burned.

water_tower_grounds_1871.text: The open lawn round the Water Tower, with shrub beds, young trees and walks. No houses stood between the tower and Chicago Avenue. A stone kerb with an iron railing ran round it.

premise: Be a hotel's young messenger on a Sunday in October 1871. Carry a note to the Opera House, then choose where to go before dark.

choices.consequence: It is the short way, right past the bell.
choices.label: Cut through the square

choices.consequence: It is longer, past the big stone offices.
choices.label: Go around by LaSalle Street

stops.narrative: Through the square, or the long way?
stops.text: It is twenty past two at the Sherman House. You tuck the note inside your coat. First, look at this hotel. It opened in July 1861. It is six floors high, and it is made of marble from Lemont. One side looks out on the big square. Now, about a famous guest. Theodore Thomas leads an orchestra. He and his players are staying here. Tomorrow night they will start ten concerts at the Opera House. Your note is going there too.

stops.narrative: The tower where the fire watchman stands.
stops.text: This is Court House Square. It fills a whole block. It has grass and trees, so it looks like a park. The building in the middle holds the city's offices. Even the jail is here, down in the basement! Now look up at the top. A twisting stair goes up to a little porch, 120 feet high. A fire watchman stands up there and looks out over the city. Tonight the watchman will be Mathias Schaffer, with his spy-glass. Now east to Washington Street.

stops.narrative: A quiet hall on a Sunday.
stops.text: This is the Chamber of Commerce, at Washington and LaSalle. It opened in 1865. Inside is a great hall with paintings on the walls. On weekdays the Board of Trade does its buying and selling in there. Today is Sunday, so it is quiet. Now, about this street. LaSalle Street is where the insurance companies have their offices, and the banks are close by. Your note is still safe in your coat. Two blocks east to the Opera House.

choices.consequence: You have never seen it up close.
choices.label: Go north to the Water Tower

choices.consequence: Lots of people have gone to look today.
choices.label: Go west to see last night's fire

stops.narrative: North to the Water Tower, or west to the smoke?
stops.text: This is Crosby's Opera House, on Washington Street. It is five floors high. Stone statues stand over the door. Shops fill the first floor, and the big theatre in back has seats for three thousand people. All summer, workers have been making it new again. The newspaper says almost every seat is sold for tomorrow night. You hand your note in at the door. Your job is done! There is still some daylight left.

stops.narrative: The stone tower and its pumps.
stops.text: This is the Water Tower, on the North Side. Across the street is the Pumping Station. Its pumps pull in clean water through a tunnel two miles out under the lake. The river is too dirty to drink. Now, about a worry. For years the fire leaders have said the city does not have enough water. All of Chicago needs these pumps, and the roof over them is made of wood. Time to go home before dark.

stops.narrative: The smoke from last night's fire.
stops.text: This is the Van Buren Street bridge. Look across the river. Last night a fire started in a mill on Canal Street. By this afternoon, four blocks had burned. Piles of coal and wood are still burning! Thousands of people have come to look. Now, about the firemen. Many of them worked for eighteen hours without stopping, and they are very tired. It has not rained for more than a week, and the wind is strong. Time to go home before dark.

title: A Message for the Opera House
